#1972. Derek McInnes will soon have a Rangers selection headache as two-striker approach assessed

Kris Boyd insists Ryan Naderi’s impressive form in front of goal has provided Derek McInnes with a selection headache he will be more than happy to have, with the striker stepping up in the absence of key attacking options.

The German forward has seized his opportunity in the starting line-up since club captain Lawrence Shankland and Youssef Chermiti were sidelined through injury, linking up effectively at the top end of the pitch with £9 million summer signing Kevin Kelsy.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The pair have struck up a potent partnership in recent weeks, playing a key part in five successive wins that have provided renewed optimism surrounding Rangers’ title credentials this season.

Former Ibrox marksman Boyd has been impressed by Naderi’s all-round game and development after starting the season well down the pecking order, although he suggests there is still room for improvement.

“There's no doubt Chermiti was going to be the one at the top end of the pitch and maybe Shankland behind him,” Boyd said. “Kelsey has come in and he and Naderi have struck up a partnership.

“Shankland will be back soon. He is different to the other two and I still think he’s the best finisher at the club. But he will have a fight on his hands getting back in the team. It’s a good problem for Rangers to have.

“At the start of the season they were creating opportunities but weren’t taking them. You do feel they can score goals, but, more importantly, this team has more of a McInnes DNA defensively. Back then they had to score two, three or four goals to win a game. Right now they can get by with a 1-0. You’d want to kill it off a lot quicker than they do, but it was another three points [on Saturday] and defensively very good.”

Boyd is an advocate of McInnes' decision to play with two strikers, having operated in that system throughout his own career. He believes the approach provides Rangers with a greater physical presence and gives the opposition more to think about.

“Overall, both of them [Kelsy and Naderi] bring so much to the team and the way Derek wants to play. He wants to get the ball forward and it's two big boys who will ask questions of defenders. Both of them have been scoring. If you wanted to ask for more it would be goals from the wider areas.

“I played that way all my career but football has changed. Derek has always wanted to have two strikers though. Even when they were struggling at Kilmarnock he’d go two up top with wingers. I do think if you are one of the best sides in the country, you can have two strikers on the pitch as long as everyone is doing their work.”

The title race remains finely balanced heading into the final international break of the year, with Celtic four points ahead despite Rangers having a game in hand.

Boyd believes McInnes will welcome the opportunity to take stock of his team’s progress, even if they have continued to find ways to collect points.

“I don’t think he will be upset about the timing of the break,” he said. “Football is about momentum but you do need that break or reset to remind the players about the run they’ve been on. You always feel the last international break to the one in the New Year is when the league starts to sort itself out. Derek will want them refreshed to kick on towards the festive period.”

#1971. Bradford City v York City: Michael Duff on pausing for breath after intense schedule

Following tonight's final EFL Trophy Northern Group C game against York City (7.30pm), the Bantams are inactive for 10 days until Saturday week, when they welcome Doncaster Rovers in a Yorkshire derby in League One.

Duff's side are already through to the next Trophy stage and only a big victory for York – already eliminated – will knock City off top spot.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

In his first three weeks in charge, City had successive midweek games to fit in. But last week's clear Saturday-to-Saturday run and their forthcoming break from action will provide some quality time on the training ground.

Duff, inset, said: "We can get some tactical element into certain things I think we need. We're not trying to change a lot, but the obvious one has been we've got the 'ten' a little bit higher in certain areas of the pitch.

"We introduced a man-to-man press against Oxford, which is something new, so you're just trying to drip a couple of new things in.

"A lot of it will be reinforcing those things, because with the schedule the way it is – and without having a pre-season where you can embed certain fundamentals – it's keeping what you've got and then dripping little bits in. It's just reminders.

"You speak to supporters, they'll probably go 'this needs to change, this needs to change'. Not that much does as it's been going all right, but certain things do need to improve."

Tonight's game is the fourth in a run of six successive fixtures – in four different competitions – at Valley Parade.

Duff added: "It helps with the travel of the players. It might not help if the results don't go so well, but the players know that anyway.

"Supporters are demanding and football drives emotion, I totally get that. They'll all go in the pub and put the world to rights, that's why everyone loves football. That's why they turn up at the weekend – to get the week's worth of venting out. Our job is sometimes you've got to suck it up and swallow it."

While the game is a 'dead-rubber' for York, who make their first competitive visit to Bradford since October 2012, there is one clear motivation with Scott Lindsey's side still waiting to record their first competitive away win since returning to the EFL.

#1970. Chichester beat Bath in Oaklands Park’s tale of two cities

The visitors came into the match in fine form with seven wins and only one loss in their previous eight league games, whereas Chi’s form has been up and down.

City made just the one change to the starting XI who won at Frome.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Skipper Rob Hutchings again lined up at left-back with Isaac Bello on the other side, with Ben Pashley and Ryan Davidson in the heart of the defence. Max Evans started between the sticks with Joe Moore, Emmett Dunn, Lucas Pattenden and Worthing loanee Matt Burgess in midfield, behind top scorer Harry Bridle and Brandon Chebby.

The visitors were awarded a free kick in the third minute but Evans collected the resulting header. Then Chebby had a shot of sorts and Bridle turned the loose ball in to put City in front.

Donovan Wilson got Bath’s leveller 11 minutes in before Callum Wood’s corner was headed away by the Chi backline.

Pattenden nearly reached a through ball ahead of Bath keeper Harvey Richards after Evans denied Oliver Chamberlain and Pashley made a couple of blocks as Bath looked to go in front.

Nice play from Pedro Elawar allowed him to find room but Chamberlain knocked the ball out for a Chi goal kick. Emmett Dunn hit a weak shot at the mid-point of the first half before Borges beat a hesitant Chi skipper Hutchings – only to blast over the bar.

Star man Chebby fizzed over a cross although no one was there to capitalise, before Evans saved from Chamberlain.

Davidson received some lengthy physio treatment just after the half-hour mark and had to be replaced by new boy Will Sweet. It tranpired Davidson had suffered a broken jaw.

Hutchings got done down the right wing by Chamberlain, who pulled a decent save out of Evans.

When Sweet was man-handled by Parsons, and after a melee, referee Joel Lamping consulted his assistant and brandished a straight red.

The visitors changed it up at the break bringing on Reuben Reid, and Bridle had a shot blocked in the first minute of the second half.

The away team thought they had gone ahead moments later through Reid but it was chalked off for offside.

Dunn headed away a corner as the away side pressed once more and Bello’s shot-cross was simple for Richards before Burgess was impeded just outside the penalty area.

Wood delivered one across the danger zone for Bath but no-one was there. A disappointing cross was easy enough for Richards before Pattenden smashed in Chebby’s fine cross on the hour to make it 2-1.

The Chi No19 might have extended the lead following a Pattenden delivery in the 68th minute, and Enzio Boldewijn’s set piece went wide. Then Pattenden’s header was saved spectacularly by Bath keeper Harvey Richards before Bridle blazed one over the bar.

The Somerset side made a triple substitution on 77, and Pattenden tried to lob the Bath keeper but it was easy for him.

Chebby fired a left-footer off target before the ball was turned out for another City corner. Clarke came on for Dunn with five minutes to go and Munt replaced Bridle.

It looked like Richards had handled outside the penalty area as we entered six minutes of additional time. And Chi should have been 3-1 up but Moore somehow missed with practically the last kick.

#1969. Aberdeen hero's sobering verdict on lost identity, Cormack's big headache and Pittodrie's revolving door

Alex McLeish reckons Aberdeen chairman Dave Cormack will be “agonising” over their current predicament, suggesting he faces a huge challenge to restore the club's standing as a powerhouse of Scottish football amid another deeply disappointing campaign.

The Dons' ongoing struggles resulted in manager Stephen Robinson being sacked on Monday, with the Northern Irishman relieved of his duties after eight months in charge as results continued to fall short of expectations.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Aberdeen’s hierarchy scheduled a hastily-arranged meeting to discuss the 51-year-old’s future in the wake of a 4-0 defeat at home to Hibs on Saturday, which left the Pittodrie side languishing in 11th place in the Scottish Premiership table.

With concerns surrounding the direction of the club, McLeish feels the problems confronting Aberdeen extend beyond the man in the dugout as he pointed towards poor recruitment, player confidence and a lack of collective identity as key issues which have all resulted in Robinson’s downfall.

Having witnessed the commitment Cormack has shown to the club, McLeish believes he will be feeling the weight of responsibility more than most after standing by his beloved team through some particularly difficult periods.

“Dave is a close friend and I know he's done everything in his power to try and get the Dons to a level,” he said. “We've seen a Scottish Cup final victory a couple of seasons ago. But the league positions are not what Aberdeen fans expect.

‘He will be agonising. You know what it’s like if you get something wrong, you can't sleep at night, can you? Dave will have been through all that kind of rigmarole as well. There'll be a big burden on him right now.

“But he's been stoic and he's stood by the club. He has to be given massive credit for that. It's just about getting Aberdeen to cement their name back at the higher echelons of Scottish football.”

That 2025 Scottish Cup triumph under Jimmy Thelin had offered hope that Aberdeen could use it as a springboard towards challenging more consistently at the top end of the league. Instead, the club have found themselves repeatedly struggling to establish the momentum required to compete with the likes of Celtic, Rangers and Hearts.

The frustration for McLeish is that the rebuilding process has yet to deliver the sustained progress supporters have been demanding.

“I've not got a solution unfortunately, but it's obviously down to acquiring players of a certain level,” he declared. “So, do they have to look at their recruitment? Is it just players that have lost their identity, lost their confidence? These are two massive factors in the world of football.”

The inevitable consequence of a prolonged run of poor results is that the manager becomes the most vulnerable figure. Robinson found himself in precisely that situation, with McLeish claiming that the pressure may have become impossible to withstand as results showed no signs of improving.

He has sympathy for Robinson, particularly given the difficulties of trying to turn around a struggling team when the responsibility for recruitment and squad construction is shared across the club.

“Is it down to recruitment? Are the players not good enough? The manager will always get the worse side of it, because they can't sack 20 players. It's sad to see. I like Stevie, I met him a few times down south and I thought he'd be good for Aberdeen. But, like everybody else, it's trying to get a team to function together.

”To have forwards that you know can score, to have midfielders that can show a bit of quality, eating a man, one-twos, being accurate with your passing. Every bit of quality factor comes into it. I'm just hoping Stevie can get a couple of good results, but it may even be too late, I don't know.”

The wider concern is Aberdeen's inability to re-establish themselves as a club opponents genuinely fear. McLeish believes fans have been waiting several years for a sustained return to prominence, with occasional moments of encouragement failing to translate into lasting progress.

“We've been waiting on it for four or five years. There's been some signs,” he reflected. “There's been obviously winning the cup that year. You think that's a wee springboard for the coming season and then it's all kind of middle of the league, lower end of the league. What is the solution? It's definitely always down to what kind of players you've got.”

#1968. 'Difficult position to be in' - Leeds United and England man Dominic Calvert-Lewin on Harry Kane competition

Leeds United star Dominic Calvert-Lewin has conceded he is in a “difficult position” behind Harry Kane in the England pecking order.

Calvert-Lewin has enjoyed a career rejuvenation at Elland Road, scoring 20 goals across 51 appearances since his arrival from Everton in the summer of 2025.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

He has catapulted himself back into the England fold, but the presence of Bayern Munich’s Kane as the country’s chief marksman presents a significant challenge for the 29-year-old.

“His record speaks for itself,” said Calvert-Lewin ahead of England’s meeting with Croatia on Thursday (November 12). “He’s a fantastic player.

“He’s the captain of the country and he leads by example. And I think he’s deserving of his accolades at the moment. On a personal note, being a centre forward in competition for that place, it’s a difficult position to be in.

“So I think when I come away on England camps now, I think I have to be just as prepared as possible and ready for when my own personal opportunity comes, if and when needed.

“I suppose it’s somewhat an audition, but it’s what I do every week that is what will warrant a call-up. Obviously you then get a chance to shine in an England shirt.”

Calvert-Lewin had gone nearly five years without an England appearance when he was ushered back into the ranks earlier this year.

Alongside him in Thomas Tuchel’s Three Lions squad is Whites goalkeeper James Trafford, who faces the task of dislodging Jordan Pickford between the sticks.

“With age, I know what my strengths are and I know what I’m good at,” said Calvert-Lewin. “Showcasing that on a weekly basis with Leeds, it’s down to Thomas if he wants to pick me or not.

“We’re both very different in the way we play. His mentality is very strong. We’re similar in that sense. We’re both very strong in how we want to play. His finishing quality, his overall quality and leadership is something I appreciate.

“Removing our own personal competition, striker watching another striker, he’s one of the best in the world and you cannot argue with that.”

England will host Croatia at Wembley on Thursday before facing Spain in Madrid on Sunday (November 15).

#1967. Only one goal but three points for the Boars: Little Common 0 – 1 Roffey

Roffey made the long journey to Little Common determined to bounce back from the unlucky defeat against East Grinstead. Pat Gibbs was rested with a niggle after his first start back for months in the previous game, Hayden Skerry is still working back to fitness and the Pearse brothers still missing through injury.

Right from the start Roffey dominated possession and the hosts sat in a low block. Callum Kilkenny had the first attempt on goal when taking a return pass from Jordan Mase before shooting over the bar. Shortly after Kilkenny got round the back and Common keeper Matt Cruttwell had to block his effort with the rebound being scrambled clear. After nine minutes Roffey thought they had a penalty for a foul on Stan Berry but after consulting his assistant, the referee ruled it out.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Eighteen minutes in with nearly all the game in the Common half, Stan Berry, back from injury, cut in from the right and fired over. Chesworth showed a wonderful bit of skill but his cross to unmarked Kilkenny was just intercepted. Next, Jack Meeres came out of the defence to play a one two, but Cruttwell saved his shot. The home side forced a free kick which was headed clear with the return cross coming to nothing. Ten minutes before half time Tom Caplin and Kilkenny combined but the dangerous cross was blocked at the near post. A corner routine led to Charlie Gibson firing in a shot that brought an excellent save from Cruttwell. The ball was cleared long, but any hope of a break was snuffed out by Teddy Wood and Kilkenny.

Thirty-eight minutes and Harrison broke down the right and cut into the area, his cross shot bringing another good save from Cruttwell. Roffey’s pressure intensified as half time approached. Berry brought another fine save from Cruttwell and Mase’s follow up was blocked a couple of yards out. The deadlock was finally broken after a slick passing combination with Chesworth and Mase, released Harrison into the box and he slid the ball inside the far post. The Boars nearly doubled the lead a minute later, but Berry’s effort was scrambled off the line.

Five minutes into the second half a flowing move down the left ended with Berry driving the ball narrowly wide into the side netting. A minute later Kilkenny had Cruttwell diving low to his right to save again. Fifty-six minutes and Mase robbed a defender but shot straight at Cruttwell. On seventy minutes Mase hit a free kick narrowly over the bar as Roffey kept the game in the Common half. Entering the last quarter of the match. Mase hit a swerving drive that brought another great save from Cruttwell. Then the keeper made a more straightforward save from a Caplin effort.

Into the last ten minutes and despite the Boars’ dominance, the lead was still only one and Roffey continued to search for the second. Mase drove over the bar then took the ball off a defender and brought yet another excellent save from Cruttwell, this time low to his left. Wood tried his luck from twenty-five yards, but the home stopper was there again. The mist was now beginning to drift over the pitch as Bailey Moyo shot high and wide. As we entered the last couple of minutes it was still all Roffey, and Wood had his shot deflected into the side netting after a free kick with Jack Meeres’ header from the resulting corner being the last significant action of the match.

Roffey took the three points against a dogged Common side backed up by some outstanding goalkeeping. Despite only scoring one goal, it was a thoroughly professional performance with the home side being denied a shot on goal throughout the ninety minutes. The Boars move back up into the play off-places and now have a ten day break before their next match v Crawley Down Gatwick at the Fusion Aviation Stadium on November 17th. At present Horsham have no game that night so it would be great to see the Lardy Army and regular Horsham supporters there, with concessions for Horsham season ticket holders. The boars are certainly playing a very entertaining brand of football.

Roffey: Burton, Harrison, Gibson, Napper, Meeres, Caplin, Wood, Mase, Chesworth(Moyo), Berry(Hoarty), Kilkenny(Allen). Subs: Skerry, Mesquita.

#1966. Romano: Milan remain obsessed with Inacio but Fonseca’s arrival could change things

It’s no secret that AC Milan will sign a defender in January, and one name is sitting firmly in the lead but he’s not alone.

Since the summer, Milan have been obsessed with the idea of signing Goncalo Inacio. His name was constant through the mercato and on deadline day, the Rossoneri tried to pounce on a last-minute deal. However, it was unsuccessful, understandably.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Within days of the mercato shutting, the Rossoneri were linked with another move in the January window and these suggestions have not gone away in the months since. Other names have been suggested, but again, Inacio remains the priority.

Speaking on his YouTube channel today, Fabrizio Romano offered an update on the club’s pursuit for Inacio ahead of the January mercato, via MilanNews.

“A defender will definitely arrive. He was supposed to arrive in the summer; he will arrive in January, so it’s no mystery. Milan also persistently sought him during the summer transfer window, an extra defender obviously in addition to Mario Gila, who was also an excellent investment by Milan, so the idea is to bring in at least another one.

“Milan reinstated Tomori a minute after the end of the summer transfer window out of necessity, but Milan’s idea is to take an extra defender. So a defender will definitely arrive.

“The name of Gonçalo Inácio must always be kept there because it is a name that has been in Milan’s mind since the first day of the summer transfer window; from when Ruben Amorim arrived until the last minute of the transfer window, he has always been in the thoughts anyway. There have been different attempts with different formulas.

“Milan had even considered, at a certain point at the end of August, a possible very expensive loan with an option to buy, so several solutions were considered that Sporting did not accept.

“Among other things, Sporting has changed its skin; Paolo Fonseca arrived on the bench, so we’ll see how much this will impact the dynamics of this operation. Clearly he’s not the only name, but Inacio is certainly a very welcome player; Milan has excellent relations with his agents, who are the same as Amorim.

“But I repeat, it doesn’t end here; there’s a list and Milan will make their choices.”

Avom’s contract is due to expire at the end of the 2026/27 season and the prospect of landing the 21-year-old in a bargain deal could prove tempting.

A central midfielder by trade, Avom is comfortable playing as a defensive anchor or as a forward-thinking playmaker.

He has made a total of 77 appearances for Lorient, scoring four goals and registering seven assists.

Luring Avom into the second tier could prove to be a difficult task, although the ambition of Boro and the Blues cannot be questioned.

Both clubs have made significant investments into their respective playing squads and are somewhat unsurpisingly sat as the second tier’s top two sides.

Birmingham went top at the weekend as Middlesbrough were held to a goalless draw by Watford, a result that left Hellberg frustrated.

He said: “Overall I’m very happy with how we’ve started the season – 14 games in, I’m happy with how brave we’ve been and how many points we have got.

“We were not good enough, or perform how we want to look, at Wrexham, and the performance here in terms of energy was so important for us.

“Of course when I look at the scoresheet and see it’s 0-0, my honest answer is that I’m very angry and disappointed over that because with all those chances created, all those beautiful attacks we had, it’s disappointing we didn’t win the game.”

#1964. Ian Hart: Champions League or a trophy for Brighton? - Why not both

At 62 I’ve been very lucky to have watched Brighton all over England, Wales and into Europe.

During various holidays I’ve also watched - on the TV - in the US, the Caribbean, Middle East. Last week it was the Far East and this week it was the Gold Coast, Australia at midnight. But why was Sunday’s victory so poignant for me?

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Not quite Saul on the Road to Damascus, but it’s another 90 minutes of realisation. It was perhaps prompted by sitting, as with Singapore last weekend, with ‘neutral’ football fans and hearing their opinions of ‘our’ football club.

It reiterates the almost seismic changes the club has undergone since that dramatic afternoon at Edgar Street in May 1997.

However somethings don’t change and I hope they never will, as the Albion’s annual commemoration of Remembrance Sunday was both poignant and fitting.

But then on to the action. The arrival of Brentford and the respective chairman’s shared backstory bubbling under in the background. Whilst not quite the M23 Derby perhaps, it’s a game we now look forward to that little bit extra.

Albion never let Brentford settle and by half time - courtesy of two goals and VAR actually doing it’s job - the Seagulls were effectively home and hosed.

So, if I had to don my mortar board and gown (Google required for some readers) and give a ‘quarter term’ report, what would it be?

Wow! Second in the table and the highest scorers in the top flight. One of the two defeats, Chelsea away, was arguably a game we should have won. And given Chelsea’s sporadic form since, if they played again this weekend, it certainty would be a different result.

Playing with flair and panache to reiterate a soundbite from previous columns, we all just have to enjoy the ride. One thing is for certain, we are in the EPL for at least another 12 months!

It’s just what will that 12 months bring. The much coveted trophy? Hopefully.

But in modern day football, what is the real gauge of success? We all want to see Dunky up on a podium lifting a pot, but what if this form continues for the remaining three-quarters of the campaign, and Albion get that all important Champions League spot?

Whether us old dyed in the wool fans like it or not, financially for the Albion that is far more lucrative than a trophy, bar the league title.

And again whilst trying not to get too carried away, there are also two huge factors coming at us over the hill. Champions League qualification, would almost certainly mean huge changes in the club’s wage structure.

If we don’t pay our squad the ‘going rate’, then rest assured somebody else in our league, and we all know the clubs, will. And naturally we would also have to recruit along with the financial implications that would bring.

Whoever you are, you can’t do the CL on the cheap! But again to reiterate, let’s not get carried away.

Many of us remember domestic football long before the advent of the ‘International Break’, but we go into this particular one in the highest league position we’ve ever been for a said break.

So let’s just enjoy every second of it, and cue dear old Doris Day… Que Sera, Sera…….only 28 games to go!

#1963. How forgotten Celtic and PSG star nearly joined Rangers as lid lifted on 'advanced negotiatons'

Former Celtic midfielder Youssouf Mulumbu has revealed how he came very close to joining Rangers after holding “advanced negotiations” with the Ibrox club.

Mulumbu joined Celtic from Kilmarnock in 2018 and spent a year at the club, making a handful of appearances. However, the DR Congo internationalist could easily have been representing the other side of the Old Firm.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

“Football is crazy,” said Mulumbu. “I'll tell you the story of how I signed for Celtic - I was actually in advanced negotiations with Rangers.

“We were finalising the contract when negotiations suddenly stalled out of nowhere. I returned to France, and out of the blue, Brendan Rodgers called me personally. He spoke to me at length about the club and how he planned to integrate me.

“Looking back, I should have shown more patience. Instead of asking to go out on loan the moment I wasn't starting, I should have stayed, fought for my place in training, and waited for my opportunity. With hindsight, had I stayed put, I would have played far more games for Celtic.

“Moving to Celtic was a dream because I had always wanted to play for an elite club competing for silverware. The dynamic was very different from Kilmarnock, though. Celtic already had established midfield leaders, Scott Brown, Callum McGregor, and Nir Bitton.

“Forcing my way into that starting lineup was difficult. We had dropped into the Europa League after missing out on Champions League qualification, but Brendan Rodgers already had a settled tactical structure and preferred starting eleven.

“It was tough to break through, but playing at Celtic Park in front of those passionate fans was a special experience. In hindsight, I feel I could and should have done more to secure regular minutes.”

Former PSG youth Mulumbu, who also had spells at Norwich City and West Brom, had a far more fruitful time at Kilmarnock under Steve Clarke, who he worked with at the Baggies.

“Kilmarnock was incredible, you know,” the 39-year-old continued. I arrived there after a bad spell at Norwich where I had lost the passion for football. But I spoke with Steve Clarke at the time, and he told me to come and enjoy my football.

“Obviously, it's not the same wages and it's not the same facilities, but I was surprised because when I arrived there, I really enjoyed training every day and playing against good sides like Celtic, Rangers, and Aberdeen. And I discovered a country as well, you know. Different mentality, different culture. It was very, very good.

“I had played five games when I arrived, and after that, I was supposed to be transferred to Bordeaux in France. I remember I spoke with Steve Clarke and I spoke with the president at the time, and they were really sad because I was doing well. And the transfer failed.”

Adding in an interview with Paris Match Casino, Mulumbu went on: “As the transfer failed on the Friday, we then played on Sunday against Celtic and I scored! All right, yeah, we won 1–0, for the story! And no, that was very, very nice mentally, you know, because after what happened at Norwich, to come back as a football player and to play for a team that loves you, where you can feel the love of the supporters and of your teammates, that was great.”

#1959. Martin Keown explains what he 'can’t quite fathom' after Leeds United's win over Tottenham Hotspur

Arsenal legend Martin Keown has conceded he “can’t quite fathom” a decision made by VAR during Leeds United’s 1-0 win over Tottenham Hotspur.

Daniel Farke’s side claimed three points at the expense of Spurs on Saturday (November 7), edging past the North London club with a late Noah Okafor winner.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

It was not a game without controversy, as many felt Whites defender Jayden Bogle was fortunate not to see red for a challenge on Spurs winger Mathys Tel.

Keown is among those who felt Bogle was fortunate and has labelled the 26-year-old’s challenge as “reckless.”

He told talKSPORT: “It looks reckless. We’re just showing the clip, we’re not seeing it in real speed. I think he’s trying to somehow line him up to tackle him with his right foot. He plants his left and his left foot goes right down the Achilles of Tel.

“Actually, as he does it, he twists his ankle at the same time. It looks out of control. I’m pretty surprised, if we’re looking for consistency, I’m a little bit surprised he hasn’t gone for that. It does look poor.

“At least it should have been a yellow. It’s the studs, it’s the full six studs isn’t it? All the way down the back of the Achilles. I can’t quite fathom how VAR looks at that and doesn’t punish.”

Tottenham are complaining to Pro Ref about the decision and Keown’s surprise has been shared by former Premier League official Graham Barber.

He said: “I thought it was a very, very poor challenge, it was reckless at best but you could describe it as dangerous and endangering the safety of the opponent, and did it endanger the safety of the opponent? Well, the answer is probably yes, because he had to leave the field of play about five minutes later.”

#1958. Scott McTominay 'had shock on heart' before Scotland World Cup game as ex-Man Utd star opens up on summer

Scotland midfielder Scott McTominay has revealed that he needed to have his heart “shocked” two days before the nation’s World Cup opener against Haiti.

McTominay explained that he was taken to hospital 48 hours before the match on June 14 and was “put to sleep”. At the time, his absence from training was put down to a sickness bug, but the 29-year-old has spoken for the first time on what he went through during the summer.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

McTominay played the full 90 minutes in the 1-0 win over the Haitians and started the next two games against Morocco and Brazil, which Scotland lost to exit the tournament at the group stage.

McTominay then went on holiday before returning to his club side Napoli, who announced on September 1 that the former Man Utd player was to have a procedure to correct a "mild benign arrhythmia". He missed the last international window under new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli, but is now back in the camp for matches against North Macedonia and Switzerland in the coming days.

“I’m good,” said McTominay in his broadcast press conference on Tuesday. “I’m feeling much, much better than I was. I feel like it was something that needed to be done. In your career you have moments like that where things like that can take you by surprise. It looks a lot worse in the media for family and friends - they see news relating to a heart issue - but it’s a relatively straightforward procedure that went really well. I’m really happy to be back and playing football again. That’s the most important thing.

“I feel like it was explained to me really, really well by the doctors at Napoli and my cardiologist in Manchester alongside the doctor in Scotland when we were away at the World Cup. He explained that if this was the case, this is how it would look. Credit to all the staff members, they made me so relaxed about the situation.”

Explaining how the World Cup unfolded, McTominay continued: “The World Cup, it was difficult for me, to be honest. I had to go and get the shock on my heart. That was two days before the Haiti game. You prepare so well, I was in such good condition and something like that happens. You’re thinking ‘how has this happened to me’. But then you have to get on with it. That’s the cards you are dealt in football. Sometimes things don’t go your way and you have to continue to do your best. It’s nowhere near an excuse but it’s something you have to look back on and say ‘well, it’s part of the process.’

“Obviously the way the World Cup went, there were at least two, three weeks of me sitting there disappointed, not quite there mentally. I needed time to settle down and have a break.

“I was 100 per cent [fitness wise], but whenever you are sat in a hospital bed two days before the World Cup, about to get put to sleep, it’s not ideal, is it? So whenever things like that happen ... it is what it is, there’s nothing you can do about it. After the World Cup, I reflected on it and I was extremely disappointed. Probably the most disappointed I’ve ever been in my career.

“After the World Cup, my summer holidays weren’t heavily centred around thinking about the World Cup, but it plays a part. Whenever you are disappointed or angry about something, you go away on your holidays and it’s just not the same. You are sat there thinking ‘we could have done more’ but that three-week break I had with my operation done me the world of good.

“I’m always one to be glass half-full but after the World Cup I was like ‘this is a tough one to take’. But you have to refresh and you have to come out stronger at the other side.”

#1955. Scott McTominay given police escort as drama 36 hours before Scotland World Cup clash laid bare

Scott McTominay has revealed he had to have a police escort to a hospital in Boston to have his heart ‘shocked’ 36 hours before Scotland’s opening World Cup game against Haiti.

At the time, his absence from training and travel arrangements to Boston – he travelled from the team’s base in Charlotte separately from the rest of the team – were attributed to a stomach bug. In fact, it was a heart condition known as atrial fibrillation.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

“You're not going to say I have something to do with my heart two days before the first game of the World Cup,” he said.

“It's not an ideal scenario being in the hospital two days before—well, technically 36 hours before the first game of the World Cup. But you have to take the cards that you're dealt on the chin. It's part of the game. There's nothing I could do about it.”

Some will question the decision to let him play in not only the match against Haiti, which Scotland won 1-0, but also the two following group games against Morocco and Brazil. The Scots lost both fixtures and exited the World Cup with McTominay perceived to have been under par.

“It was in my hands,” he said. “The medical team reassured me it was safe to play and they said: ‘What do you think?' I said: ‘Let’s go for it’.”

Unbeknown to nearly everyone, and while Scotland fans were drinking bars dry in Boston, McTominay was at the centre of incredible drama.

Manager Steve Clarke told reporters that the midfielder had been laid low by a stomach bug. The reality of the situation - and the fact it was kept secret for so long - is barely believable given the global attention on the tournament and that McTominay is Scotland's star player.

He himself sought to downplay the situation on Tuesday at Hampden as he revealed the true story for the first time. “We got a police escort to go and get the shock then that was it to be honest,” recalled McTominay. “After that, I was back in normal rhythm, which is how a healthy heart should be then I went and played the game two days later.”

He described being put under anaesthetic. “You have to get put to sleep,” he said. “Whenever you go under anaesthetic and you have to get put to sleep, it decreases the athletic performance a little bit and (affects) sleep and stuff like that. It was far from ideal but those are the cards that you're dealt, there's nothing you can do about it.”

Although he stressed his family were fully on board with him playing, he wouldn’t have listened had it been otherwise. “All my family and friends had just flown 10 hours for the first game of the World Cup,” he said.

“I didn’t sit there thinking I might not play. That would never be the case. I was always going to play in that game. Maybe selfishly, I don’t know but that’s football. Players play with injuries all the time when they’re not quite right and it might be to the detriment of the team. (But) I was fully functional.”

The Napoli midfielder has since undergone an operation after the problem resurfaced following an early season Serie A game against Como. He returned to Manchester, where he had a procedure known as pulsed field ablation.

The player was sidelined for several weeks, missing the first games under new Scotland manager Sebastien Pocognoli but has returned to the squad for upcoming Nations League games against North Macedonia and Switzerland.

#1954. Former Leeds, Sunderland and Crystal Palace striker and ex-Bristol City midfielder join Crawley Town

Both join on short-term deals ending in early January.

Bringing a wealth of experience from the very highest levels of English football, Wickham arrives with an outstanding footballing pedigree, having represented some of the country's most established clubs, including Sunderland, Crystal Palace, Ipswich Town, Sheffield Wednesday, Leeds United, Cardiff City and Charlton Athletic.

The 33-year-old began his professional career at Ipswich, making his first-team debut at just 16 years old and becoming the club's youngest-ever player at the time. His impressive performances quickly attracted attention from Premier League clubs, eventually earning him a move to Sunderland in 2011.

During his time at Sunderland, Wickham established himself in the Premier League and played a crucial role in the Black Cats' remarkable survival during the 2013-14 campaign. His goals against Manchester City, Chelsea and Cardiff helped secure vital points, earning him the prestigious Premier League Player of the Month award in April 2014.

Throughout his career, the powerful forward has also enjoyed spells with Sheffield Wednesday, Leeds, Preston North End, MK Dons, Forest Green Rovers, Cardiff and Charlton, gaining extensive experience across the Premier League and English Football League.

Benarous arrives with experience in the EFL Championship and League One, having previously represented Bristol City and Plymouth Argyle, as well as earning international recognition with England at Under-17 level.

Born in Bristol, the 23-year-old joined his boyhood club Bristol City at just six years old, progressing through the club's academy ranks before signing his first professional contract in February 2021, aged 17.

After leaving Bristol City in the summer of 2025, the midfielder joined Plymouth Argyle, adding further senior experience in League One and domestic cup competitions to his footballing CV.

Deals for Wickham and Benarous are both subject to the usual EFL and FA Approvals.

#1953. AC Milan 0-2 Ferencvaros: Five things we learned – a poor squad picked apart

AC Milan’s Europa League misery continued at San Siro on Thursday night as they were beaten 2-0 by Ferencvaros.

Ruben Amorim made six changes to the team that won the derby against Inter, hoping that the entire group would remain buoyed by that performance to secure a much-needed win in Europe. However, what followed was the worst performance of his tenure so far.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Lenny Joseph netted twice in the second half to capitalise on errors and fire the Hungarian side to a memorable win. Ferencvaros were not even rocked by a red card to the substitute Yusuf as they kept the Rossoneri at bay quite easily, securing a two-goal win they deserved.

The result means that Milan have now dropped out of even the top 24 spots, and they can just about say goodbye to any hopes of direct last-16 qualification barring a miracle. Ivan Stoev has five things we learned from another dismal midweek game.

It’s difficult to pick five talking points after a game like this, as we can probably spend quite a bit of time discussing how bad each of the players were. But let’s try to address the bigger issue.

This squad is full of sheep, lacking both leaders and the quality to compete. We can talk all about how much Amorim rotates the squad and try to ease the blow by suggesting the Rossoneri didn’t field their best XI. Yet, if the management were serious about making the club competitive, then the rotational players should be above the quality of almost all teams competing in the Europa League, bar a few.

Obviously, if we assume Amorim is the right choice and Gerry Cardinale is serious, then it will take a lot more than a single transfer window and three new players to get Milan to compete on a few fronts, which was further proven against Ferencvaros.

Out of the whole squad, the only player that can change a game is Diego Moreira, who doesn’t play every game and has lots of room for improvement still. Not to mention that playing with the likes of Filippo Terracciano, Ardon Jashari and even Goncalo Ramos is not helping Belgium at all.

The rest of the squad lack either the quality or the mentality. The collective arrogance on the pitch was insufferable to watch, with Ferencvaros looking like the only side that had any desire to actually win. Whilst the Diavolo looked like they were playing a game in the park with no aggression, no focus, no intensity. No nothing.

It’s a bit pointless to discuss individuals because I think the wider point is clear – Milan lack leaders, Milan lack quality and Milan lack a game changer that can get the ball and make something happen when the tough gets going.

It was made evident after four games in the Europa League and a few blunders in Serie A that there’s lots of work to be done in January and next summer.

Again, it’s difficult to pick and choose which player to discuss, but given Ramos is the Rossoneri’s most expensive signing ever, it’s probably fair that the pressure starts mounting on him.

Listen, I wasn’t too bothered by the lack of goals initially, as the striker did well in the build-up and opened up space for his teammates; he also ran a lot in both phases of the game. Let’s also be honest, he has lacked the service to actually get the goal-scoring opportunities.

Nevertheless, in the last few games and especially against Ferencvaros, he has been dire – his build-up is poor, his ball control is pretty bad and when he does get a shot off, it’s usually miles away.

Now, obviously he’s not a striker that’s going to create chances for himself; he lacks the pace and the trickery, which is fine if you are good in the other aspects of the game. However, we can’t keep grasping for straws.

The reality is that the former PSG man is just not living up to the expectations given the hefty sum paid for him in the summer.

In retrospect, maybe it wasn’t wise to spend such a sum on a player who needs quality around him in order to be a better facilitator or to receive more chances overall. The reality as of now is that the Portuguese is a disappointment.

Again, as we said, most players in the squad lack quality or mentality and unfortunately for us there are some that lack both and it’s way past the tipping point at this stage.

Terracciano, for starters, has not shown anything worth mentioning in all of his games with the red and black shirt and there’s really no reason for him to get minutes. Even without pressure, he’s just not of the needed level.

Jashari is another one that the fans and the management have hoped will bounce back after his lengthy injury after joining Milan. Yet, he’s probably had one good game from start to finish and there’s always gaps in his game.

It’s probably wise at this point to accept he’s not going to live up to the expectations and a solution needs to be found on the market, especially given Luka Modric will most likely be retiring at the end of the season.

There are also other players in this category that didn’t necessarily participate in last night’s game but should have the same fate – Pervis Estupinan and Ruben Loftus-Cheek to name a couple.

If nothing else, these poor performances should highlight to the management where the gap in quality is and what the strategy on the transfer market should be.

4. De Winter’s disastrous performance proves costly

I think the biggest individual call-out should definitely be the Belgian, who played an awful back pass to Lorenzo Torriani on the first goal. Yes, the keeper could’ve and should’ve done much better, but that back pass was just so sloppy – it could put an outfield player in a tricky situation, let alone a goalkeeper that perhaps isn’t as comfortable with his feet.

This especially coming from a player who should’ve been a certainty at the back given the heavily rotated squad.

We can also partly criticise the intervention on the second goal, because it started the whole sequence leading to the Joseph’s brace. Yes, it was a bit unlucky where the ball ended up, but you can also argue it was sloppy, the same way you can argue that a keeper clearing the ball into the opponent’s feet after a shot instead of towards the corner is the keeper’s fault to an extent.

It’s just unacceptable to go from bullying Thuram to being bullied by not even Ferencvaros’s first-choice striker.

5. Amorim’s tactics fail, but the players also struggle

I think it’s probably fair to criticise the Portuguese coach a bit too, as the Hungarians totally outplayed the Diavolo at the San Siro and were tactically better. All in all, they had the answer to everything Milan tried to offer on the night.

At the same time, I’m torn to put the blame fully on Ruben Amorim because he did make a triple change at half-time, bringing on Pulisic, Moreira and Gila, which was still at 0-0. At that point, the Rossoneri had more than enough quality on the pitch to be able to deal with whatever Ferencvaros had to offer.

Instead, two individual mistakes gave away the opening goal and it all went downhill from there. Even after the red card, Milan struggled to create a big chance.

I personally struggle to blame this fully on tactics given all the circumstances and we are back to the point that the Milan squad are just not good enough and lacks that killer mentality.

#1952. Scott McTominay: I didn't know what people were saying about me and the World Cup

Picture the scene. Scotland fans are drinking Boston’s bars dry. Meanwhile, unbeknown to them, their star player, their main hope, was getting a police escort to a hospital in the city to have his heartbeat jolted back into a normal pattern. Scotland tend to make a drama out of World Cups, but this is something else.

It is almost a year to the day since Scott McTominay wowed the world with an overhead kick to set Scotland on the way to qualifying for the tournament for the first time in 28 years against Denmark. This might have been expected to be a main topic of conversation as the player sat down for an all-too rare interview at Hampden on Tuesday.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

In the end, however, this scintillating piece of skill, immortalised on a tenement gable end near Hampden, proved barely an afterthought. McTominay consents to interviews only very infrequently, certainly in Scotland. When he does do them, they seem like events.

This is especially the case when he is recalling being blue lighted through the streets of Boston a couple of evenings before Scotland were due to make their long-awaited return to the World Cup against Haiti.

It is scarcely believable that having had his heart effectively reset, he was lining up against the Caribbean nation in a pulsating World Cup encounter a mere 36 hours later. He very nearly even scored.

The Napoli midfielder watched a shot crash off the post in the first half shortly before John McGinn scored with a deflected effort that proved the winner. Although he was so close to getting on the scoresheet, the general perception was that McTominay struggled to shake off the effects of the “stomach bug” that had been communicated as the reason for his absence from training two days beforehand.

The midfielder was considered never to have reached the heights expected of him during Scotland’s tournament, which lasted another two games. It must have been excruciatingly irritating for him to read such verdicts and be unable to respond.

He was even rated in some quarters as among the tournament’s biggest flops. The Scotland staff couldn’t say anything, nor could he. He claims he was oblivious to the criticism.

“I didn’t know that’s what people were saying,” he said. “Although I probably had an idea. I’ve been criticised a million times before in my career before but I don’t let it get under my skin or worry too much about it.

“You know yourself as a professional footballer if you’re not quite where you should be. For me, I had half an idea but you just try to block it out because if you think about negative things you might speak it into existence.”

There might be a lot of people eating humble pie having been informed of the true nature of McTominay’s health problem. It’s no one’s fault. You can’t refer to such a serious mitigating factor if it’s being – understandably – kept hidden. McTominay explained to rapt reporters the details behind his condition, which is known as atrial fibrillation. In other words, an unsteady heartbeat. He even provided some sound effects. Who says McTominay is an unwilling interviewee?

“Atrial fibrillation is a fairly normal routine thing for people in general,” he said. “They might not know that they have it. But when you're an elite athlete in general across the board, across football, across sports in general, you know if you've got something that's different.

“Whenever you're running and you check your pulse and it's got a slight irregular beat there, it feels like your heart's coming out of your chest.

“Not obviously as bad as that but that's the sensation that you have. It's pumping, but not a regular heartbeat like bum, bum, bum, bum. Mine's going bum, bu-bu-bum, bum, bu-bu-bum. So you know the difference.”

You also know that it’s not something you would wish to develop on the eve of the World Cup that is being played in intense temperatures.

“The heat was tough, that was probably the hardest part,” he reflected. “But I’ve worked for 20 years as a young footballer and as a professional to get to that point, to try and play well at a World Cup.” Nothing, he stressed, was going to stop him, not even lying on a hospital bed under anaesthetic two evenings before the first game while an electrode is placed on his chest.

He has since been back in hospital for a more involved procedure. Napoli released a statement in September to say the minimally invasive operation known as cardiac ablation surgery had been “a complete success” although McTominay missed several matches, including the first four Nations League fixtures under new manager Sebastien Pocognoli.

“I went into that surgery with no doubt in my mind that I’d be back,” he said. “I lost a little bit of muscle when I came out, three or four kilos which wasn’t ideal. I had to put that back on pretty sharpish.

“The first picture of me when I came back, I looked quite gaunt. So I had to get that muscle back so I could get back my powerful running and what I normally do on a football pitch.

“It was a good reset period for me,” he added. “No matter how long it took - even if it took until I was 40! - I was coming back to try and do my best. I’ve had a good time to reflect on the World Cup and think about things leading up to it.

“When I had the operation I had three weeks at home. I didn’t watch as much football as I normally do. I (normally) watch every game of football, every night. It’s relentless with me.

“Games in the Champions League, Europa League, Scottish football, the Premier League, Serie A - I watch a lot now compared to when I was younger.

“So I had three weeks of resting my mind more than anything to try and come back in a better state.”

It’s good news for the Tartan Army, who are desperate for McTominay, who turns 30 next month, to rescue Scotland from an unsure start to the Nations League under Pocognoli. The Belgian has stressed he wants to find a way of taking the burden off those such as McTominay. But the player himself doesn’t mind the extra responsibility. Indeed, he relishes it.

“He's mentioned that to me before about maybe taking a little bit (of the burden) and putting it across the whole board, but I don’t see football like that,” he said.

“I don’t go into a game thinking that the people watching really need me to do something here so I try to do different things, you just play the game, don’t you?

“Express yourself and play how you would normally play, and the rest will take care of itself, you don’t need to overthink about pressure.

“I’ve played at Man United, I’ve played at Napoli, I know what pressure is. I’ve played for Scotland in the World Cup, I know what pressure is. It’s not the worst thing in the world that can happen to you. It’s a privilege to have things expected of you.”

Pocognoli told reporters last week that he was looking forward to making a connection with someone generally identified as Scotland’s star player. It seems he is already well on the way to achieving this despite the pair only having met in the flesh for the first time earlier this week.

It was Pocognoli's idea for McTominay to sit down with the media at Hampden on Tuesday, an instruction he obeyed.

“I like his ideas a lot,” said McTominay “Whenever I first had a meeting with him, I liked the way that he wants to play the game.”

At the end of the near 15-minute conversation with McTominay, an annual at best occurrence, there was just about enough time to reference the approaching one-year anniversary of That goal. And mention That 36ft tall mural, which was unveiled earlier this year.

“Unreal,” he said. “I don’t know how I feel. I obviously like it, it’s incredible, but if you were asking me, you don’t want my big ugly face up there!”

#1951. Leeds United given injury update on Gabriel Gudmundsson by Sweden boss Graham Potter

Leeds United defender Gabriel Gudmundsson could train with Sweden this week - despite being forced out of action with a hamstring injury at the weekend.

The 27-year-old is a key cog in Daniel Farke’s Leeds machine but had to be withdrawn midway through the meeting with Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday (November 7).

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

He was replaced at left wing-back by Melvin Bard, who produced a strong performance to help the Whites clinch a 1-0 win.

International duty with Sweden now calls for Gudmundsson, who looks set to be back on the pitch this week.

Sweden boss Graham Potter told Fotbollskanalen: “He's okay. The X-ray went well, but we need to see him and go through a couple of days of recovery to make sure he's okay.

“He'll probably be on the field with the guys on Wednesday-Thursday. There's no problem.”

When asked if Gudmundsson could start against Bosnia & Herzegovina on Saturday (November 14), Potter replied: “Yes.”

Gudmundsson could come up against a familiar face, with his Leeds teammate Tarik Muharemović a key figure in the Bosnia ranks.

Sweden will be on their travels after hosting Bosnia, visiting Poland next Tuesday (November 17).

Leeds paid a reported £10m to prise Gudmundsson from French outfit Lille in the summer of 2025 and he has proven to be an incredibly shrewd addition.

His form has kept Bard on the fringes, although the former France youth international staked a claim for more regular action with his impressive outing against Spurs.

Bard said: “[The manager told me] to play like I did in training - to defend well, also to attack and just to enjoy myself.

“I think I made a good entrance. It was also important to get into the match well, because the team had played a good first half. And also, Gabi had played a good first half, I’m thinking of him too, because he got injured. I think I made a good entrance.”

#1950. Alexander Isak starts to justify £125m price tag with double

There was a centre-forward who played for Newcastle a couple of years ago. Do you remember him? He was as quick as greased lightning, played on his instincts, had a shot like cannon and could come up with a finish for every situation.

Everyone wanted him, but Liverpool signed him for £125m in August 2025. His name was Alexander Isak but shortly after arriving on Merseyside, it was like he went missing, as the guy who played in red last season bore only a physical resemblance to the guy who had played in black-and-white.

If you had wondered what had happened to him, he reappeared at Portman Road. They say good things come to those who wait. Although nobody at Liverpool would have expected such a delay to see the real Isak, there were no complaints that his career at the club has finally taken off.

Taking the headlines from Bradley Barcola on a big night at Portman Road was going to take some doing, but Isak did just that with a double salvo in the opening nine minutes, a flurry so potent it was like a boxer charging out of their corner and seeing the first blows land flush on their opponent’s jaw.

Poor Ipswich. There is universal recognition that Liverpool are a team – and a club – in transition but they had four players in Isak, Florian Wirtz, Cody Gakpo and Victor Muñoz who had the potential to dismantle the hosts if they clicked and that is precisely what happened.

“With Alex, it is clear,” said Andoni Iraola. “If he is fit, if he is available, if he is in a good shape, he will produce the numbers. My demand with Alex will not be about the goals. It will be about other things so we can play well. And if we play well, we are in good positions. Then goals will come.”

So for all the noisy backing they received from the stands and for all the effort Gary O’Neil’s side put into a contest that TV companies had chosen to broadcast because there was a potential for drama, Isak blew a hole in Ipswich’s hull in the sixth minute and they were submerging from there on in.

A blistering finish from Alexander Isak! 💥 pic.twitter.com/jSGlIZsQtA

How Isak, who had scored against Nottingham Forest last weekend, needed a night like this when he made a genuine difference. But the same was true, too, for Iraola. We live in an era where someone has to be in the eye of a storm and the Basque will know what comes with his new territory.

It had clearly irritated Iraola that Liverpool had gone behind four times in their opening two fixtures and during his pre-match media briefing, he effectively gave a sermon at one point on how slow starts, or giving the opposition a helping hand, would no longer be tolerated.

Quietly, Iraola is making his presence felt. The task he faces is significantly different than the one O’Neil is accomplishing – keeping Ipswich in the division against the odds – but Liverpool’s head coach is a man who knows his own mind and is not afraid to make decisions.

He had responded to criticism of his midfield at Newcastle on the opening weekend by dropping Ryan Gravenberch for the fixture with Forest and his response to scrutiny about his right-back seven days ago was to drop Jeremie Frimpong and bring in Ronald Araújo.

Iraola certainly picked the right team: Araújo, the loan capture from Barcelona, added stature to the back four and there was harmony in how they moved. The Uruguayan’s first instinct was to stay back and Liverpool looked better for it, even if O’Neil, incredibly, felt Ipswich had the better of things.

Emersonn, Ipswich’s Brazilian striker, did not see the ball in the opening exchanges and, by the time he did, Liverpool had zoomed into the distance to such an extent that you felt it was going to be impossible for them to peg their visitors back.

“I hate having to talk about good performances when you do not get points,” O’Neil declared to a room full of raised eyebrows and you can only assume his message was to ensure that morale in the dressing room was not drooping.

What damage was inflicted with Liverpool’s first significant attack. Gakpo, the subject of an £80m bid from Manchester City, was never going to allow transfer speculation to disrupt his focus and he nudged a perfect little ball into Isak’s path in the sixth minute to show his wellbeing.

The next move announced the return of Isak. One touch gave him an avenue to shoot, the next was a shot with his right foot that was so hard from 16 yards, on an angle, it bent the wrists of Kjell Scherpen as it howled into the net. Critics will feel Ipswich’s keeper should have done better.

Your first thought was to think of the first goal Isak scored in English football in September 2022, a similarly venomous drive, against Liverpool at Anfield. He oozed quality that evening, his pace and skill had Jürgen Klopp’s defenders persistently fretting and this is what he was doing again.

It was no coincidence that three minutes later, he came up with another wonderful goal. This one owed much to the beautiful pass Gakpo presented to him, an inch-perfect through ball with the outside of his right foot, but Isak still showed great poise to bamboozle Scherpen.

Inside NINE minutes Alexander Isak has two goals! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/3UGq0bwqRm

“He owes me a few assists now!” chirped the selfless Gakpo.

A hat-trick could have arrived in the 32nd minute but Isak was a kneecap offside as he dispatched a pass from Wirtz and, perhaps, he will have been disappointed to have made way on the hour having not secured the match ball for his efforts.

Liverpool, too, will be frustrated that they did not made sure of three points before the time Isak made way for Barcola – what Alexis Mac Alliser was thinking when he fluffed an unmarked header from six yards, only he will know – but it was not a night to nitpick.

There will be easier assignments on the horizon for Ipswich, even though O’Neil insisted they more than held their own against world-class opponents. And you can say for sure there will be more goals and wins for Liverpool and Isak if they continue in this encouraging manner.

“I witnessed what a great coach he was at Bournemouth. He is not the sort of manager you are going to see making clever patterns in his box. He just does not see the risk. He will want to get the ball to the players who want to make a difference. Coaches do not show how good they are by how they play out from the back. The important thing is when you get it in the final third, you make things happen. That is what he will want to improve. He will want Alexander Isak when he has not got the ball to press. He will want the same of Florian Wirtz. The difficulty will come with Champions League football and not putting too many demands on his players. If he gets it right, he has got a wonderful squad to work with.”

"My demands will not be about the goals, my fights with him are about other stuff." Andoni Iraola speaking about Alexander Isak 🔊 pic.twitter.com/B4zUG2IGfS

“He has had good minutes, a good pass in a counter, a good couple of chances when he was going against the goalkeeper and we have not found him. We need to learn these movements because he will be there threatening in behind all the team. But he looks confident on the ball as always. He had not played any competitive minutes since the World Cup so we had to be a little bit more careful.”

"Yeah, that's nice" 😁Alexander Isak talks through his second goal vs Ipswich 🔍 pic.twitter.com/diG2xv50Bw

“We were waiting for the first win, and we were talking about starting the game well, which we have not done recently. And we did that with two goals. With a normal pre-season, I think we are starting to get the way we want to play, being offensive and attack the defence. We showed that today. We scored two and could have scored more.

“It was not easy. It was a long injury, a difficult season [last season] in general. I was thinking; I want to have a good World Cup firstly and then to start the season well, which I feel like I have done now. That season is kind of behind me, but it was not easy.”

Cody Gakpo was linked with both Tottenham and Manchester City during the transfer window but stayed at Liverpool and has been in good form in these first three games of the season. He has assisted all three of Alexander Isak’s goals so far.

4 - Cody Gakpo has been directly involved in four goals in the Premier League this season (1 goal, 3 assists). This century, only Mo Salah in 2024-25 has had more goal involvements through Liverpool's opening three games of a league campaign (6).Retained. pic.twitter.com/hGN0NpF5A3

“You have to believe in yourself and have the belief of the fans that you are the man when you come for that much money. He had a terrible injury last year, but you can hear the Liverpool fans. They absolutely love what they saw. Some of his skills, his movement. That comes from his goal last week and the confidence that brings. Fingers crossed he can carry this on.”

The Swede’s two early goals have earned Liverpool all three points at Portman Road and the travelling Liverpool fans are singing his name. Isak’s fellow teammates are pushing him towards the travelling fans to take their adulation as they belt out his name.

The final whistle goes at Portman Road and Andoni Iraola picks up his first win as Liverpool boss with a 2-0 victory thanks to Isak’s quickfire double inside the opening 10 minutes. Like they did two seasons ago, Liverpool win 2-0 at Portman Road.

Enciso has a late shot from the edge of the box but it goes wide of the far post.

McAteer shoots from range but there is not enough power to trouble Alisson, who makes the save down to his right.

A late change from Liverpool as Koumas replaces Wirtz.

Due to that VAR review for the Liverpool penalty that was not, there will probably be five or six added minutes.

Clarke’s shot from just outside the Liverpool penalty area takes a deflection off his teammate Diop and goes wide.

Davis is getting a fair bit of joy down Ipswich’s left and the ball has been on to him quite a few times. He is being afforded too much space by Liverpool to get crosses in.

Andoni Iraola is bringing on Nyoni for Mac Allister, who was on a booking.

Davis is found making a run in behind and his cross from the left side of the box is blocked by Araujo and goes behind for a corner. Lukic’s delivery is headed away at the front post by Gravenberch.

Double change for Ipswich as McAteer and Ouattara replace Fatawau and Palacios.

Barcola drives down Liverpool’s left and, as he approaches the Ipswich box, cuts onto his right and feeds it across to Gakpo, whose shot misses the target.

The ball comes to Flemming on the edge of the box and he tries to curl one into the far corner but it is an easy save for Alisson.

Barcola is nearly played in behind but Scherpen does really to get out of his goal quickly and gets to the ball first, just ahead of Barcola.

Davis and Ipswich can count themselves very, very lucky. It would have been a penalty but Szoboszlai was offside when the original ball was played. For the second time tonight, an offside call massively goes in Ipswich’s favour; one to deny Isak a hat-trick and now to deny Liverpool a penalty. A massive let-off for Ipswich.
